summary: The batched strategy works: the winding checks out for hulls, arcs and rims, raycasting is off and geometry is disposed. The biggest remaining gain is in terrain. Convex hulls around concave hex districts overlap each other at the same y (-0.055), which causes z-fighting and crossing borders. Next in impact: 1px transparent lines still look like a wireframe, the readiness rails run into each other across sectors, and three transparent instanced layers have no fixed draw order. I recommend three fixes: exact hex-cell district regions with ribbon outlines, readiness rails with gaps and tick marks, and a more deterministic prism edge and target layering.
design:
What's already correct: hullTriangles reverses counter-clockwise hulls so they face up (in XZ, y-normal = -cross2d). Both arc triangles face up, and hexRimGeometry faces up and lines up with CylinderGeometry. Watch out: the per-cell footprint loop (sin a, cos a) runs clockwise in math-XZ, so a hex made that way must be passed to hullTriangles reversed.

1. District regions as a union of cells instead of a convex hull (terrain; biggest gain). Give each cell a hex footprint with circumradius R = pitch/√3, where pitch is the nearest-neighbour distance within the district. Pick the phase so footprints tile: the vertex at 0 from +z needs neighbours along ±x, otherwise set phase = π/6. Hash each undirected edge by its quantized endpoints. An edge seen twice is interior; edges seen once form the concave outline. The result has no overlap between districts, a true cartographic shape, and costs about 6k edges.

2. Replace the lineSegments with opaque world-width ribbons. Width is about 0.07·cell, or 0.12·cell for the selected root. Use a precomputed colour, surfaceBright lerped toward outlineStrong by 0.65, so there's no blending. Merge the ground, outlines and rails into one vertexColors mesh (one draw call) using the y-layers -0.055, -0.03, +0.03. This also covers the constellation sector borders.

3. Measured readiness arcs. Pad each sector by gap = min(0.25·span, 0.35/R) so neighbouring rails read as separate gauges. Draw the status-colour fill at full width over [s, fillEnd] and a thin hairline track only over [fillEnd, e]. They don't overlap, so there's no z-fight between 0.025 and 0.035. Add ticks at 25/50/75% outside the band. When total = 0, draw a lighter track so it reads differently from 0%. The 2D twin must mirror the gaps and ticks.

4. Prisms. Make the crowns opaque, with the instance colour set to unitColor lerped toward onSurface by 0.22. That leaves only glass and target rim as transparent layers: set renderOrder glass = 1 and target = 2. Glass is one colour at one alpha, so blending is order-independent and unsorted instances are fine. Scale glass to 0 when there is no gap. Use a separate target rim, hexRimGeometry(0.8), so it survives on small screens. Call computeBoundingSphere only when the animation settles (moving = false), not every frame.
risks: These are inferences from source only; no visual captures were supplied. Tune ribbon widths and lerp amounts against real screenshots.
The cell union assumes each district is on a regular hex lattice. If the packing is jittered, edge hashing will leave slivers. In that case, fall back to the hull, inset per district.
Getting the lattice phase wrong gives gaps or overlaps. Add a test that a two-cell district has exactly 10 outline edges.
Rail gaps and ticks change the 2D twin's appearance, so mirror them there and keep the fill proportion measured over the padded span.
Opaque crowns lose the translucent tint, so check lens colour contrast against the tokens.
Merging everything into one mesh relies on y-separation of at least 0.01 for depth. Check near/far planes on large catalogs.
Rebuilding geometry when the selection changes is still a full rebuild. It's cheap at 1014 units, but could later become a colour-only attribute update.
